The training loss is: L_normal = mean(max(0, threshold − s_i)²) (push normal scores below threshold), L_anom = mean(max(0, s_i − threshold)²) for the highest-scoring window (push at least one window above threshold). A weakly-supervised assumption: the model learns that the highest-scoring window in an anomaly clip corresponds to the actual anomaly event. At test time, a frame-level anomaly score is computed from the sliding windows, and a threshold triggers an alert. No frame-level annotation is needed; the model infers temporal localization from weak clip-level labels.

No Need for Real Anomaly — MLLM Zero-Sho.narr: Anomaly models require retraining on new environments and new anomaly types. Multimodal language models carry broad common-sense about normal and abnormal behavior. An MLLM zero-shot detector describes the scene in natural language and judges whether it matches a normal context, flagging deviations without any anomaly training data.
No Need for Real Anomaly — MLLM Zero-Sho.how: The mechanism: Sample a frame from the video; query the MLLM: "Describe the people and actions in this scene." The model outputs a natural-language description, e.g., "A pedestrian walking on a street." Next, ask the MLLM: "Is this description normal? Would you expect to see this in a typical city scene?" The model outputs a confidence score for normality. Repeat for several frames. Abnormal frames get low normality scores. Smooth scores temporally (Kalman filter) and threshold to generate anomaly alerts. The MLLM's common-sense about the physical world (e.g., people don't usually walk backward at high speed, objects don't usually float) serves as the normality model. No retraining is needed for new locations or new anomaly types; the MLLM generalizes because it learned normality from internet-scale training. Trade-off: zero-shot MLLM detection may have more false positives than a trained model, but it requires zero annotation.

CC-STAR — Contact-State Anomaly Detectio.narr: Assembly anomalies (part misalignment, wrong gripper state) are detected by force and tactile feedback, not vision. A temporal state machine learns normal contact sequences during assembly (gripper open → touch part → apply force → release) and flags deviations as anomalies.
CC-STAR — Contact-State Anomaly Detectio.how: The mechanism: Sensors measure 6D force (Fx, Fy, Fz, Τx, Τy, Τz) and tactile pressure at each finger. At each timestep, compute a contact state: 0 = gripper open/no contact, 1 = touch (pressure > threshold but force < threshold), 2 = grasp (pressure > threshold and force > threshold), 3 = insert (Z-force spike), etc. A sequence model (LSTM or HMM) is trained on normal assembly trajectories to predict the next state. At test time, if the observed state diverges from the predicted state, flag anomaly. Example: after step 3 (insert), the model expects state 4 (release); if the Z-force continues rising (state 3 persists), the part may be stuck or misaligned. The model learns that normal sequences have characteristic durations and force profiles; anomalies break these patterns.

RAID — Retrieval-Augmented Anomaly Detec.narr: A single normality model may not capture all normal behaviors across time and conditions. Retrieval-augmented detection stores a bank of normal video prototypes and compares each test clip to the nearest prototypes, flagging large deviations at test time without retraining.
RAID — Retrieval-Augmented Anomaly Detec.how: The mechanism: Build a prototype bank: during training on normal videos, encode each clip c_i → e_i ∈ ℝ^{128} via a pretrained encoder. Store all embeddings and optionally a low-resolution thumbnail. At test time, encode the test clip c_test → e_test. Compute similarity to all prototypes: sim_j = cos(e_test, e_j). Retrieve the top-K nearest prototypes (K=5). Compute anomaly score as: anomaly = 1 − max_j sim_j (if most similar is far, it's anomalous). Alternatively, fit a Gaussian to the top-K similarities and compute a z-score. The benefit: new environments or seasons can be added without retraining—just add new normal prototypes to the bank. The trade-off: storage grows with the number of normal scenarios; retrieval is O(N) for N prototypes. Approximate nearest neighbor (FAISS) speeds this up.

GEM — Generative Environment Model from.narr: RGB future prediction struggles with occlusion; LiDAR captures 3D structure. A LiDAR-conditioned world model predicts future 3D point clouds by learning scene geometry and agent motion, enabling planning without hallucinating invisible regions.
GEM — Generative Environment Model from.how: The mechanism: Encoder: A LiDAR point cloud P_t ∈ ℝ^{N×3} is voxelized into a 3D grid V_t ∈ ℝ^{X×Y×Z×C}. A 3D CNN encodes V_t → z_t ∈ ℝ^D. Dynamics: An MLP predicts the latent state at the next timestep: ẑ_{t+1} = f_θ(z_t, a_t) where a_t is the ego-vehicle's action (steering, acceleration). Decoder: ẑ_{t+1} is decoded back into a point cloud P̂_{t+1} via transposed 3D convolution. Loss: chamfer distance between predicted and ground-truth clouds. Why it works: LiDAR penetrates occlusion (though it sees fewer points behind dense objects), so the model learns which regions are likely occupied based on geometry. Unlike RGB, there is no "blur the uncertain parts"—the point cloud is sparse, forcing the model to learn coherent 3D motion. For planning, sample action sequences, predict futures, and score each with a reward model (e.g., collision cost, distance to goal).

NavForesee — Vision-Language World Model.narr: Navigation planning often relies on reactive control; long-horizon planning requires predicting where a goal is reachable. A vision-language world model predicts future visual observations conditioned on language goals, enabling a robot to simulate reaching the goal before committing to a path.
NavForesee — Vision-Language World Model.how: The mechanism: Encoder: A camera frame x_t and language goal "go to the kitchen" are encoded jointly via a multimodal encoder. Latent state z_t ∈ ℝ^D captures the current visual-semantic state. Dynamics: An LSTM or diffusion model predicts: z_{t+1} = f_θ(z_t, a_t, language_embedding). Action a_t is the robot's motion command (forward, turn, etc.). Decoder: z_{t+1} → predicted frame x̂_{t+1} via a vision decoder (e.g., VAE decoder). Planning: Given a goal, roll out H predictions in imagination: sample a_1, ..., a_H to generate predicted frames x̂_1, ..., x̂_H. Score each rollout with a "goal achievement" metric: sim(x̂_H, goal_image) or an MLLM query "Does this image show a kitchen?". Pick the action sequence with the highest score. The language grounding ensures the model learns to predict visual changes that move toward the goal, not just any plausible future.

Dynamics Modeling for High-Speed Off-Roa.narr: Terrain dynamics (sand, mud, rocks) affect traction and handling; modeling them from vision alone enables fast adaptation. A video-prediction world model learns terrain-specific dynamics by predicting ego-vehicle camera frames, inferring the underlying terrain response from visual motion cues.
Dynamics Modeling for High-Speed Off-Roa.how: The mechanism: Input: a sequence of front-facing camera frames from high-speed off-road driving. The vehicle is equipped with IMU and motor encoders to label the true ego-motion. Model: An encoder compresses frames into a latent state z_t. A dynamics model predicts z_{t+1} = f_θ(z_t, a_t, terrain_embedding) where a_t is steering/throttle and terrain_embedding is learned per terrain type (or predicted from visual features). A decoder reconstructs x̂_{t+1}. Loss: L2 between predicted and true frames. The model implicitly learns terrain friction, slip angle, and inertia because these affect how pixels move in the next frame. Example: on sand, a hard left turn produces more slip; the model learns this by observing the discrepancy between steering angle and visual rotation. For control, the learned model predicts outcomes of actions; choose the action that leads to the best predicted state (e.g., max speed while staying on terrain).

Envisioning the Future One Step at a Tim.narr: Diffusion and VAE world models are flexible but expensive; autoregressive models are fast and deterministic. A causal autoregressive video prediction model generates future frames one-by-one, each step conditioned on all previous frames, serving as a substrate for planning without sampling uncertainty.
Envisioning the Future One Step at a Tim.how: The mechanism: At each timestep t, the model predicts frame x_t given the history x_1, ..., x_{t−1}: x̂_t = decoder(f_θ(encoder(x_1), ..., encoder(x_{t−1}))). The encoder is a CNN or Vision Transformer that extracts features from the history. The decoder is an autoregressive transformer that generates x̂_t token-by-token (after quantization to discrete tokens using VQ-VAE or similar). Loss: cross-entropy between predicted and true tokens. At test time, given an initial sequence x_1, ..., x_k, iteratively generate x̂_{k+1}, then x̂_{k+2} conditioned on x_{k+1}, and so on. For planning: given a reward model r(x_t, a_t), use beam search or Monte Carlo tree search to find the action sequence that maximizes cumulative reward. Because the model is deterministic, there is no randomness; the predicted trajectory is the single most-likely future. This determinism is useful for planning: the model commits to one trajectory, not sampling multiple futures.
